According to pathological findings, patients were divided into two groups: DSI ≥1/2 and DSI <1/2. Normally distributed continuous variables were compared using independent-samples t-tests, whereas skewed variables were compared using non-parametric tests. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to assess the sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC) of ADC, APT, DCE-MRI parameters, and their combination for predicting DSI. Diagnostic performance was compared using the DeLong test. RESULTS: A total of 61 patients were included, with 33 in the DSI <1/2 group and 28 in the DSI (≥1/2) group. The ADC values were significantly lower in the DSI ≥1/2 group compared to the DSI <1/2 group (P < 0.01). In contrast, APT, maximum relative enhancement (MRE), and wash-in rate (WIR) values were significantly higher in the DSI ≥1/2 group (all P < 0.05). The AUCs for APT, ADC, MRE, WIR, and their combination in predicting DSI were 0.73 (95% CI: 0.60-0.83), 0.71 (95% CI: 0.58-0.82), 0.70 (95% CI: 0.57-0.81), 0.68 (95% CI: 0.55-0.80), and 0.85 (95% CI: 0.73-0.93), respectively. Moreover, combining APT, ADC, MRE, and WIR yielded significantly improved diagnostic performance over each parameter alone (P < 0.05). CONCLUSION: APT imaging is useful for predicting DSI in early-stage cervical cancer before surgery. When combined with ADC and DCE-MRI parameters, its diagnostic accuracy is further improved. This multimodal imaging approach may offer a more reliable method for preoperative assessment of stromal invasion in early-stage cervical cancer.

articles.title: Multicenter external validation of a multimodal MRI deep-learning model to predict meningioma bone invasion.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Preoperative detection of meningioma bone invasion lacks objective biomarkers and relies on subjective radiological assessment, posing a risk of excessive bone resection or residual tumor. We therefore developed and externally validated a parsimonious six-feature DenseNet121 signature derived from multiparametric MRI across two independent institutions. METHODS: In this retrospective diagnostic accuracy study, 438 consecutive patients (mean age, 53 ± 11 years; 77% women) with histologically confirmed meningioma were allocated to training (n = 182), internal validation (n = 77), and external test (n = 179) sets. Following N4 bias-field correction and isotropic resampling, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and diffusion-weighted volumes were fed into a DenseNet121 architecture to extract a six-feature signature via nested cross-validation. Discrimination (area under the ROC curve, AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and clinical utility (decision-curve analysis) were evaluated. RESULTS: In the external cohort (prevalence 11%), the signature achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.73-0.91), sensitivity 75%, specificity 77% and negative predictive value 96%, with an AUC improvement of 0.155 over conventional radiomics (95% CI, 0.01-0.30; p = 0.035). At a 20% risk threshold, decision-curve analysis confirmed a positive net clinical benefit, primarily driven by the high negative predictive value. SHAP analysis demonstrated the dominant and consistent contribution of low-ADC features. CONCLUSION: The DenseNet121-derived six-feature signature serves as a reliable rule-out aid for preoperative meningioma bone invasion, with a high negative predictive value that may safely support decisions to avoid extensive bone resection in predicted-negative cases. Positive predictions require confirmatory CT or intraoperative biopsy to mitigate false positives. This tool could assist nurses and surgeons in preoperative planning, facilitating personalized patient care and potentially reducing operative time and complications.

articles.title: A multimodal MRI-based study of early-stage Parkinson's disease across age-at-onset groups.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate distinct iron deposition and neurite microstructural alterations in deep gray matter nuclei between early-onset Parkinson's disease (EOPD) and late-onset Parkinson's disease (LOPD) patients using quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI), and to evaluate the ability of these quantitative metrics to distinguish EOPD and LOPD from their corresponding healthy controls. METHODS: Fifty-three early-stage PD patients (15 EOPD and 38 LOPD) and 58 healthy controls (17 young healthy controls and 41 older healthy controls) underwent multimodal MRI. QSM-derived magnetic susceptibility and NODDI-derived parameters (NDI, Viso, ODI) were analyzed in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr), red nucleus (RN), globus pallidus (GP), putamen (PT), and caudate nucleus (CN). RESULTS: In EOPD, the iron content in deep gray matter nuclei was not significantly different from that in young healthy controls, but ODI was reduced in the left SNc. In LOPD, increased QSM values were observed in bilateral SNc, PT, and left CN, alongside decreased NDI and increased Viso in the left SNc, and reduced ODI in bilateral SNc and PT. Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that the combination of the NDI and ODI in the left SNc could effectively differentiate patients with EOPD from young healthy controls, whereas the optimal combination for distinguishing patients with LOPD from older healthy controls consisted of the NDI, ODI, and QSM in the left SNc. CONCLUSION: Multimodal MRI revealed distinct spatial involvement patterns in early-stage EOPD and LOPD and showed potential for distinguishing PD patients from their corresponding healthy controls.

articles.title: A hierarchical residual Swin transformer with dual-level locality compensation for accelerated MRI reconstruction.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides high spatial resolution, excellent soft-tissue contrast, and reliable anatomical discrimination, and is therefore widely used in clinical diagnosis. However, long acquisition time still limits imaging efficiency and clinical throughput. Although convolutional neural network (CNN)-based deep learning approaches have shown considerable promise for reconstructing images from undersampled k-space data, existing methods frequently fail to preserve fine structural details and texture continuity under aggressive undersampling conditions. In this study, we propose a novel reconstruction network based on the Swin Transformer, which integrates three key components: (i) long residual connections to facilitate the recovery of high-frequency details; (ii) a dual-level locality compensation mechanism to restore local spatial information; and (iii) a channel recalibration module to explicitly capture global dependencies among channels, thereby enhancing global feature extraction. Extensive experiments conducted on the IXI and MICCAI 2013 datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms several compared generative adversarial network (GAN)-based approaches for MRI reconstruction across all undersampling mask types, achieving a PSNR improvement of approximately 0.6-1 dB over the best competing method under various settings. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/cvgjhuor/HR-SwinGAN.

articles.title: Native T1 mapping versus myocardial perfusion reserve index for coronary microvascular dysfunction detection in patients with ischaemia and nonobstructive coronary artery disease: positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging validation.
articles.abstract: AIM: Native T1 mapping has not been systematically compared with the myocardial perfusion reserve index (MPRI) for detecting coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMVD) in patients with ischaemia and nonobstructive coronary artery disease (INOCA). The aim of this study was to investigate the diagnostic performance of native T1 mapping and MPRI for detecting CMVD compared with positron emission tomography (PET)-derived myocardial flow reserve (MFR). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Seventy-seven INOCA patients underwent stress/rest PET/magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), including 3-T native T1 mapping and gadopentetate dimeglumine perfusion MRI. CMVD was defined as PET-derived MFR <2.0. MPRI was calculated using CVI42 software, with native T1 values analysed via endocardial/epicardial contouring. RESULTS: CMVD patients had significantly higher mean global native T1 values (1238 ± 25 milliseconds vs 1200 ± 21 milliseconds; P < .001) and lower MPRI (1.68 ± 0.34 vs 2.14 ± 0.36; P < .001). Native T1 inversely correlated with global (r = -0.57; P < .001) and regional MFR (r = -0.53; P < .001), and MPRI significantly correlated with global (r = 0.58; P < .001) and regional MFR (r = 0.46; P < .001). Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed comparable diagnostic accuracy between native T1 and MPRI (P = .310). At a cutoff of 1225 milliseconds, native T1 mapping showed 72.7% sensitivity and 93.2% specificity, while MPRI (cutoff <1.99) demonstrated 84.9% sensitivity and 70.5% specificity. CONCLUSION: Native T1 mapping correlates inversely with MFR and matches MPRI for CMVD detection in INOCA. This gadolinium-free technique enables safe serial monitoring, particularly for renal-impaired patients, and may serve as a robust surrogate for CMVD severity.
